sentences: This is Las Meninas by Diego Velázquez.
On a canvas more than three metres tall, a little princess, her maids, a court dwarf and a large dog gather in a room of the Spanish royal palace.
At first glance it looks like an ordinary moment at court.
The fair-haired girl standing in the light at the centre is the Infanta Margarita.
She was five years old, the daughter of King Philip IV and Queen Mariana, and at that time their only surviving child.
On the left, a kneeling maid of honor offers the princess a small red cup on a golden tray.
On the right, another is just about to curtsy.
These young ladies-in-waiting, the meninas, give the painting its name.
Before the huge canvas on the left, holding brush and palette, stands Velázquez himself in a self-portrait.
Court painter and chamberlain of the palace, he has paused in his work and looks straight out at us.
The red cross on his chest is the emblem of the Order of Santiago.
Velázquez was only knighted in 1659, so the cross was added three years after the painting was finished, a late honour written onto his own portrait.
Now look at the small mirror in the middle of the back wall.
The king and queen appear in it, faint and blurred.
So whoever the painter is portraying, and wherever we are standing, it is the place of the king and queen.
To the right of the mirror, a man pauses on the steps of an open doorway, silhouetted against bright light.
He is José Nieto, the queen's chamberlain, whose job was to open and close doors for her.
Through him, the room seems to go on and on.
In the right foreground stand the court dwarfs Mari Bárbola and Nicolás Pertusato.
The boy playfully nudges the sleepy mastiff with his foot.
The dog, unbothered, keeps its eyes half closed.
The room is in the Alcázar palace in Madrid, where Velázquez had his studio.
Light from the windows on the right and shadow deepening toward the back create a powerful illusion that we are standing in the same room.
By scrambling the roles of viewer, viewed and painter, the picture has kept philosophers and artists arguing for centuries.
The painter Luca Giordano called it the theology of painting, and in 1957 Picasso made 58 versions of his own.
Step back now and meet the painter's gaze.
Are the people in this room looking at the king and queen, or at you, standing right here in front of the painting?
Stay in that spot for a moment and see how it feels.
